Today in AI NOW & BEYOND 🔥 RAG That Actually Understands Tables, Charts, and Diagrams Mother Says Meta AI Dug Into Her Children’s Details and Location AI Highlights of the Week Too Important to Miss RAG That Actually Understands Tables, Charts, and Diagrams Most RAG pipelines struggle when documents contain more than plain text. Tables lose their structure, charts get skipped, and diagrams don't translate well into embeddings. VultronRetriever brings multimodal retrieval to RAG with open-weight models that treat PDF pages as images, preserving visual context while using late-interaction retrieval to find the most relevant pages. With strong ViDoRe V3 results, you can self-host the models or run them through Vultr Serverless Inference. See VultronRetriever in Action! Mother Says Meta AI Dug Into Her Children’s Details and Location The company says it fixed intrusive prompts after a family video triggered unexpected questions Kalie Robins shared a video of herself singing with her daughter. She says Meta AI then suggested questions that pulled together personal information from years of family posts. Key Points: Her Children’s Details: The chatbot gathered names, birth information and photos of both daughters, including material posted by relatives. A Search for Home: Robins says it suggested asking where she lived, then connected older and newer posts to pinpoint her location. A Photo She Thought Was Gone: Robins says the chatbot also resurfaced a picture she had deleted years earlier. Meta Acknowledges the Problem: Meta says it fixed the inappropriate suggestions, while stressing that answers only draw on information the user can already access. Why It Matters: The privacy concern is not just what people share, but what AI can piece together from it. A birthday post, an old photo, and a family video can reveal far more together than their owners intended. 79203.subject: Circle’s Missing Funnel
79203.body:
View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/eaa70932-7ce4-467e-b338-a662ed575d6a/0xR_NL_Banner_Heading_Wordmark.jpg?t=1776775276)
Caption: 

Happy Wednesday! Today we look at Arc's public mainnet and why renting distribution from multi-chain apps is not the same as owning the funnel that made Robinhood Chain work. Elsewhere, the CLARITY Act failed to clear cloture in a 49–50 vote and took crypto with it. BTC fell 3.2% to near $75.9k, with the tail off as much as 9.2%.

———————————————————————————

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/42e942ec-f31d-4957-8722-a3ac7b121e1e/0xR_NL_Market_Update.png?t=1767631151) [Market Update]
Caption: 

Crypto sold off on the Senate’s failed cloture vote on the [Digital Asset Market Clarity (CLARITY) Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/3633/text). The motion received 49 votes in favor and 50 against, short of the 60 needed to advance. Every index we track fell on the session except Meme, which gained 1.0%. BTC lost 3.2% to near $75.9k against the S&P 500 at -0.4% and the NASDAQ 100 at -0.6%, and the tail took the worst of it: Low Revenue, High FDV (-9.2%), Modular (-8.5%), DePIN (-7.9%), and Bittensor Ecosystem (-7.2%).

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/2853175e-88e2-4730-a95b-667604b9b25e/image.png?t=1789545010)
Caption: 

The weekly tape concentrates the damage in crypto. The S&P 500 fell 0.2%, the NASDAQ 100 fell 0.9%, gold fell 1.9%, and BTC fell 3.6%, while most crypto indices fell 5% to 20%. Republicans Josh Hawley, Susan Collins, and Jerry Moran joined Democrats in voting against cloture; Thom Tillis switched from yes to no for procedural reasons so he could move to reconsider the vote. Democratic negotiators said the remaining dispute centered on stronger ethics restrictions on officials’ crypto holdings. [Polymarket odds](https://polymarket.com/event/clarity-act-signed-into-law-in-2026) on enactment this year fell from 34% on Monday to 5%.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/6d26fc45-e34a-4e5a-9c56-f1796814d4f8/image.png?t=1789545010)
Caption: 

Near-term federal crypto policy now shifts back toward agency rulemaking. The SEC and CFTC continue to advance crypto policy under existing authority, the OCC says it expects to finalize GENIUS Act stablecoin rules by November, and FASB’s proposal on when certain digital assets can qualify as cash equivalents is open for comment through November 19. Agency action is generally less durable than statute because future commissions can revise or rescind rules through new rulemaking, subject to administrative-law constraints.
